newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Black Americans urged to help Africa's revival.
newsitem.headline: Black Americans urged to help Africa's revival.

text.p: African leaders urged black Americans on Thursday to lobby corporations and the U.S. government for investment, pledging in turn to promote democracy and peace in the world's poorest continent.

"Preach the gospel of a new Africa -- of new leaders who are prepared to take advantage of the dividend of peace," Swaziland's King Mswati told delegates to the four-day African/African American summit in Zimbabwe's capital Harare.
Namibian President Sam Nujoma, saying it was time for "action, not excuses", said the continent's leaders would not allow the hoped-for "African Renaissance" to fail.

"We cannot afford to fail at the point where our continent is at the threshold of success," he said. "If we fail...we will have killed hope itself, and our failure will give rise to the inevitable consequences which are too ghastly to contemplate."

President Yoweri Museveni of Uganda, referring to investor perceptions of Africa as war-prone and unstable, said many of the continent's conflicts were a legacy of colonialism but added they did not necessarily contradict the growing shift toward political freedoms and democracy.
"That simplistic approach of looking at all wars as unnecessary is not correct," he said. "Peace under oppression is not acceptable. The other word for peace under oppression is submission."

Mapping out the continent's revival, African Development Bank President Omar Kabbaj said economic reforms were paying off with the continent's aggregate growth up from an average of 1.6 percent for the period 1990-1994 to 4.8 percent in 1996.

"The political landscape in Africa is undergoing a sea of change. While serious political problems continue to afflict some countries, the quest for democracy, peace and security is having a profoundly beneficial impact," he said.

Interspersing their speeches with repeated references to Africa as the "homeland" of black Americans, the African leaders won applause but no public pledges following their appeals for direct investment in manufacturing, technology and infrastructure.
At least one U.S. delegate responded to the calls.
Former Republican member of Congress and Secretary of Housing Jack Kemp said: "I feel too that I am home because this is the home of civilisation".

Sentimentally dubbing the conference "a summit of humanity", he pronounced that it was time for a Marshall-type plan for Africa and said while he no longer had any authority in the White House he would lobby for Africa.

"I plan to tell the American people and my party... to get busy building trade and investment in Africa," Kemp said. "It will be on partnership terms -- not patronising or paternalistic as it has been in the past."
The Marshall Plan was a U.S.-financed aid programme which helped to revive Western Europe's economy after the ravages of World War Two.
